title: The Crystalline Field Parameters for Dysprosium Ethyl Sulphate
contribution: Fitted crystal-field parameter values with slight temperature variation; serious disagreement with the Elliott-Stevens extrapolation; empirical variation with atomic number contrasting with their prediction (abstract).
problem_entry: Determine the four crystal-field parameters of Dy3+ in the ethyl sulphate (abstract).
key_idea: Fit the parameters at 4.2 K and 58 K to the known level splittings and g values (abstract); fitting procedure not read.
positioning: Contradicts Elliott and Stevens; agrees with Judd's earlier work on europium ethyl sulphate (abstract). Trajectory (inferred): parameter fitting to data is the problem shape of his later least-squares work (S012); the fitting method is not stated.

quotes.text: These values are, however, in serious disagreement with those obtained by the extrapolation procedure of Elliott and Stevens.
An empirical variation of V_n^m with atomic number is given which is in marked contrast to that predicted by Elliott and Stevens.

title: An iterative method for finding stationary values of a function of several variables
contribution: New iterative method for stationary values with second-order convergence (abstract); no experiments mentioned.

quotes.text: In many ways it is similar to the method of steepest descents; however this new method has second order convergence.

title: Crystalline-field splittings in cerous magnesium nitrate
contribution: Six-coefficient C3v crystal-field fit suggests the simple ionic model is incomplete; omitted factors listed but undecided; estimate of first excited doublet energy agreeing with spin-lattice relaxation measurements (abstract).

key_idea: Fit six coefficients of a C3v crystal field on one 4f electron; a similar analysis of Hellwege's wider-temperature data reaches the same conclusion (abstract).

quotes.text: the relative magnitudes of the six coefficients which fit the data suggest that a simple ionic crystal field model does not in fact describe the properties completely

title: An efficient method for finding the minimum of a function of several variables without calculating derivatives
contribution: Derivative-free conjugate-direction method; satisfactory practical applications; numerical examples up to twenty variables (abstract); no convergence theorem mentioned.
problem_entry: Derivative-free minimization, entering from the well-known one-parameter-at-a-time method (abstract).
key_idea: Two variations of the classical method: one makes it choose conjugate directions on a quadratic (fast ultimate rate), a further one makes convergence from a bad approximation efficient (abstract). Secondary: cycles of n or n+1 line searches; the dropped direction maximizes the determinant 'natural measure' (S014 pp. 20-21).
experiments: Numerical examples with functions of up to twenty variables (abstract); details not read.
positioning: Secondary: improved on a conjugate-direction method of Smith (R007 p. 6).
limits_future: Secondary: Powell later worried that the direction choice may drop directions already conjugate (S014 pp. 44-45); cited by him as successful without good theoretical justification (X001 p. 17).

method_links.note: claim rests on practical use and numerical examples with a stated size range (up to 20 variables)
minimal variations of a classical method rather than of his own predecessor
early instance: 1964 direction exchange maximizes a determinant (secondary)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: two-part design: model-case change for the local rate plus a separate change for progress from a bad start
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: conjugacy on quadratics gives fast ultimate rate; a further variation handles bad starting approximations; same split stated for the 1968 hybrid method (S019 p. 6)

transferable: Present a new method as named, separate changes to a well-known method: one change gives the right behaviour on the quadratic model problem (conjugate directions), the other handles starts far from the solution, so each can be judged on its own (abstract).

quotes.text: This variation is such that when the procedure is applied to a quadratic form, it causes conjugate directions to be chosen, so the ultimate rate of convergence is fast when the method is used to minimize a general function.
Practical applications of the procedure have proved to be very satisfactory, and numerical examples are given in which functions of up to twenty variables are minimized.

title: A method for minimizing a sum of squares of non-linear functions without calculating derivatives
contribution: Derivative-free sum-of-squares method with convergence comparable to the classical least-squares generalization; evaluations roughly proportional to n; 50 equations in 50 unknowns solved with fewer than 200 evaluations (abstract).
problem_entry: The classical generalization of linear least squares (Gauss-Newton) is efficient for sums of squares but needs derivatives (abstract).
key_idea: An original method with comparable convergence that needs no derivatives (abstract); mechanism not read.
experiments: One large concrete test: fifty nonlinear equations in fifty unknowns, fewer than two hundred evaluations (abstract).
positioning: Secondary: Powell (2005) says the 1965 least-squares method without derivatives is also used often in practice (X001 p. 12).

method_links.note: cost measured in function evaluations against n (about O(n)), as Method 3 step 5 prescribes
headline claim is one concrete large test with an exact evaluation count
keeps the classical procedure's convergence and removes one requirement (derivatives); base is a classical method

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: same benefit as the classical technique, one requirement fewer
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: comparable convergence to the classical procedure without derivatives; second instance S062

transferable: State a derivative-free method's efficiency as evaluations relative to n and back it with one large concrete instance and its exact budget (n = 50, fewer than 200 evaluations), not an average over small problems (abstract).

quotes.text: The number of times the individual terms of the sum of squares have to be calculated is approximately proportional to the number of variables.
Finding a solution to a set of fifty non-linear equations in fifty unknowns required the left-hand sides of the equations to be worked out fewer than two hundred times.

title: On the maximum errors of polynomial approximations defined by interpolation and by least squares criteria

quotes.text: It is proved that the maximum errors of approximations defined by interpolation and by least squares criteria are within factors, independent of f(x), of the least maximum error that can be achieved.

The resultant numbers are not large: for example, if interpolation is used to evaluate a polynomial approximation of degree 20 it may be guaranteed that the resultant maximum error does not exceed the minimax error by more than a factor of four.
